body_markdown:
COVID-19 infections are rising across all 50 US states during summer 2026. Learn why experts are concerned, which regions are most affected, and how to stay protected.


For years, Americans associated COVID-19 with winter outbreaks, crowded indoor gatherings, and the traditional cold and flu season. However, new data suggests that the virus is no longer following the patterns many people have come to expect. Instead, health experts are increasingly observing a second major peak during the warmer months.


Recent surveillance data indicates that COVID-19 infections are growing or likely growing across all 50 states. While overall respiratory illness activity remains relatively low compared to the early pandemic years, public health officials are closely monitoring the latest increase, particularly in the southern and western regions of the country.


## COVID Is No Longer Just a Winter Concern


The coronavirus has evolved from an emergency pandemic threat into an endemic virus that circulates throughout the year. Yet many people still associate COVID-19 with winter.


According to disease experts, the United States has developed a pattern of two annual COVID waves: one during late summer and another during winter. This shift means that rising infection rates in August and September are no longer unexpected.


Health officials note that current infection trends are increasing nationwide, even though emergency department visits and severe illness levels remain significantly lower than the peaks experienced in previous years.[\[cdc.gov\]](https://www.cdc.gov/cfa-modeling-and-forecasting/rt-estimates/index.html?ref=private-content.ghost.io) ,[\[localsyr.com\]](https://www.localsyr.com/news/national/covid-is-growing-in-nearly-every-state-cdc-reports-heres-where-levels-are-highest/?ref=private-content.ghost.io)


## Cases Increasing Across All States


The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that COVID-19 infections are growing or likely growing in every US state as of mid-August 2026. This marks a notable shift from earlier in the summer when transmission levels were far lower.


While national activity remains categorized as low or very low, experts emphasize that trends matter just as much as current levels. Rising infections can translate into increased transmission in schools, workplaces, and community settings as people resume regular activities and students return to classrooms.


Several monitoring systems, including wastewater surveillance programs, have detected steady increases in viral activity since late June. Some researchers report that viral concentrations in wastewater have risen substantially compared to early summer levels.


## Why the South and West Are Seeing Higher Growth


Public health experts have identified the South and West as the regions experiencing the most significant increases in transmission.


According to CDC outlook models, these regions entered summer with comparatively lower levels of recent population immunity following a milder winter COVID season. As a result, more people remained susceptible to infection when summer transmission began to rise.


States throughout these regions are showing higher wastewater activity and stronger growth patterns than many parts of the Midwest and Northeast. Although hospitalization rates remain manageable, experts continue to monitor potential changes as transmission increases.


## Will the Summer Surge Continue?


Many infectious disease specialists believe the current wave has not yet reached its highest point.


Researchers tracking COVID transmission patterns expect activity to continue climbing into early September before reaching a peak. Factors such as travel, large gatherings, back-to-school events, and indoor social interactions can contribute to continued spread.


Although the current increase appears less severe than some previous waves, experts caution against interpreting lower hospitalization numbers as evidence that the virus no longer poses risks. COVID-19 can still lead to serious complications, particularly among vulnerable populations.


## Who Remains Most Vulnerable?


For most healthy individuals, current infections may result in relatively mild illness. However, some groups remain at elevated risk for severe outcomes.


These include:


- Older adults
- People with weakened immune systems
- Pregnant women
- Individuals with chronic health conditions
- Young children


Medical professionals continue to recommend extra precautions for these groups, especially during periods of increasing community transmission.


Additionally, concerns remain regarding long COVID, which can affect some people even after their initial infection has resolved. Symptoms may persist for weeks or months and can impact daily functioning and quality of life.


## Vaccine Discussions Are Returning This Fall


As COVID activity rises, attention is once again turning to vaccination.


An updated COVID-19 vaccine targeting currently circulating variants is expected to become available during the fall vaccination season. Public health organizations and medical societies continue to support vaccination as a tool for reducing the risk of severe disease and hospitalization.


However, vaccination rates have declined compared to earlier years, reflecting pandemic fatigue and changing public perceptions of risk. Health experts stress that individuals should discuss vaccination options with their healthcare providers, particularly if they belong to a higher-risk category.


## How to Protect Yourself During Rising COVID Activity


While broad public restrictions are no longer in place, experts continue to recommend practical measures that can help reduce transmission:


1. Stay up to date with recommended vaccines.
2. Consider testing if symptoms develop.
3. Avoid close contact with others when sick.
4. Improve indoor ventilation whenever possible.
5. Follow guidance from healthcare professionals regarding personal risk factors.


These simple strategies may help reduce the spread of respiratory viruses during periods of elevated community activity.


## Final Thoughts


The latest rise in COVID-19 infections highlights an important reality: the virus is still circulating and adapting to new seasonal patterns. What was once seen primarily as a winter illness is increasingly producing significant summer activity as well.


Although current infection levels are far below the most severe stages of the pandemic, the ongoing increase across all 50 states serves as a reminder that COVID-19 remains a public health concern. Staying informed, understanding personal risk, and following evidence-based medical guidance can help individuals make informed decisions as the fall season approaches.
